## The mug is not psychologically invisible

You meet someone while holding a cozy mug versus an icy can. In some lab setups, that body feeling spills into how "warm" or trustworthy the person seems.[^1][^2] Holding something warm can bias first impressions. Effects on real choices show up in some studies—but they are not magic, and they are not always easy to replicate.

Think of a brain neighborhood that tracks **both** "my hand is warm" and "that person seems warm." Researchers often name that neighborhood the **[anterior insular cortex](../../glossary.qmd#anterior-insular-cortex)** (sometimes just "the insula"). The everyday idea—body state as a tint on social judgment—is what psychologists call **[embodied cognition](../../glossary.qmd#embodied-cognition)** when they want a lab label. You do not need either label to follow the open story.[^1][^2]

Why does this lesson sit between monasteries and ritual breaks? Because Chapter 5's decision games will ask you to take "warmth" seriously as a *confound*—and as a bridge. If mug temperature can shift first impressions, then a decision study that forgets temperature may mix pharmacology with thermal priming. Careful protocols later lock cups near **60°C ± 2°C** for exactly that reason (see [Chapter 5 · Section 4 Study protocols](../module-05/04-study-protocols.qmd)).

## What the early studies claimed

Williams and Bargh (2008) reported that people who briefly held a warm cup of coffee rated a stranger as having a "warmer" personality than people who held an iced cup, and that holding a warm (versus cold) therapeutic pad raised the chance of choosing a gift for a friend rather than for oneself.[^1]

Follow-on imaging work linked physical and social "warmth" in that same hand-warmth / social-warmth brain neighborhood: overlapping activation when people experience warm pads and when they read warm, supportive social messages.[^2] Kang and colleagues reported that physical temperature also shifted responses to fairness and trust allocations in bargaining settings.[^3]

A warm cup can nudge first impressions and opening trust in cited work. It does not guarantee generosity forever. The lab numbers, condition tables, and effect sizes live in the foldouts below—open them when you want the poster detail.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: condition table and original warmth numbers"}
| Condition | Stimulus | Typical behavioral skew in cited work | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Warm prime | Warm insulated cup / hot coffee briefly held | Partners rated warmer/more trustworthy; more friend-oriented gift choice in original Study 2 | Williams & Bargh (2008) [^1] |
| Cold prime | Iced cup / cold pad | Partners framed as colder/distant; more self-oriented choice | Williams & Bargh (2008); Inagaki & Eisenberger (2013) [^1][^2] |
| Warm mug in Trust / fairness settings | Warm ~60°C mug (narrative of Kang et al.) | Higher first-mover investment / fairness sensitivity in cited designs | Kang et al. (2011) [^3] |

| Measure | Warm | Cold / control | Trail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Personality "warmth" (1–7) | M ≈ **5.63** | M ≈ **4.04** | Williams & Bargh (2008) [^1] |
| Gift for friend vs self | **54%** friend | **75%** self | Williams & Bargh Study 2 [^1] |
| Trust / fairness first send | ~**+24.8%** vs cold (~$7.85 vs $6.29 of $10) | Cold pad ~10°C | Kang et al. (2011 source) [^3] |
| fMRI overlap | Bilateral anterior insula cluster during warm pad + supportive messages | — | Inagaki & Eisenberger (2013) [^2] |

Read these as **lab snapshots**, not personality transplants. The original Williams & Bargh behavioral effect size was remarkably large (*d* ≈ 1.69 in one reading of Study 1)—large enough that later replications treated it as a claim that needed a hard check.
:::

## Replication honesty (keep this clear)

People sometimes say: "Warm mug always makes people generous." Williams & Bargh (2008) reported a very large effect. A large preregistered multi-lab replication of Study 2 (Lynott et al., 2014; total **N = 861** across three sites) **failed** to copy the pure behavioral gift-choice result.[^4] Later independent reports have also found near-zero effects for the original warmth-to-prosocial link.[^5]

What looks more robust in the sources' framing is the **neurobiological overlap** in that hand-warmth / social-warmth brain neighborhood between physical warmth and social bonding—shown in imaging and thermoregulation-style designs.[^2] Downstream behavior in unstructured settings depends on person, attachment style, and ambient room temperature (source note).

That honesty is part of the story: interesting claim → checked claim → limited claim.

::: {.callout-caution title="Warmth is interesting—not a boardroom cheat code"}
Lynott et al. (2014) did not replicate Williams & Bargh's Study 2 gift-choice effect at any site or in the combined N = 861 analysis.[^4] Keep that in view when someone sells "serve tea, win the deal." Opening trust nudges in *some* cited designs (including Kang's temperature manipulation) are still worth knowing—especially as a reason Chapter 5 locks mug temperature—but they are not a permanent negotiation upgrade.[^3][^7]
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: what failed to replicate—and what still matters for later chapters"}
**Failed / fragile (behavioral gift choice).** Lynott et al. (2014): three high-powered labs, combined N = 861, no support for brief warm-pad → prosocial gift choice.[^4] Chabris and colleagues' later reports likewise lean near-zero for the original warmth-to-prosocial headline.[^5]

**More durable (neural overlap claim).** Inagaki & Eisenberger (2013): shared anterior insula responses to physical warmth and social warmth cues.[^2]

**Still useful as a methods warning.** If thermal primes can shift *some* social and fairness behaviors in *some* designs,[^3] then decision studies that ignore cup temperature risk mixing chemistry with warmth. That is why [Chapter 5 · Section 4 Study protocols](../module-05/04-study-protocols.qmd) specify opaque mugs near **60°C ± 2°C**.

This warmth thread reappears in [Chapter 5 · Section 3 Trust games](../module-05/03-trust-games.qmd)—the same first-mover figure is one of the bridges on [Linkages](../../linkages.qmd).
:::

## Passive warmth vs active ritual

Warmth, in this lesson, is mostly **passive**: you hold something hot or cold. Ritual, in the next lesson, is **active**: you *make* the tea on purpose—measure, watch, wait. Both can sit beside "calm trust" talk. They are not the same mechanism.

A warm cup can nudge first impressions and opening trust in cited work. A familiar brewing sequence tries to interrupt anxious looping with predictable steps. Keep both tools—and keep both caveats.


## A beginner picture of the hand-warmth / social-warmth overlap

You do not need a neuroscience degree for the sources' core image. One brain neighborhood helps track both "my hand is warm" and "that person seems warm/trustworthy." When those maps overlap, a hot mug can briefly color a social judgment.[^2] Lab papers often name that neighborhood the **anterior insular cortex**—the foldout below keeps the coordinates.

That is the embodied-cognition idea in one sentence: body state as a tint on social paint.

Important limits, said early and often:

- Tint is not destiny.
- Lab tint is not boardroom strategy.
- Early behavioral headlines were large; later replications were not.[^4]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: where physical warmth and social warmth meet"}
Inagaki and Eisenberger (2013) used fMRI to look for overlap between physical warmth (warm vs cold pad) and social warmth (reading supportive messages). They report a shared cluster in the **bilateral anterior insula**—the sources' teaching coordinates are about **x = 38, y = 20, z = −4** in that paper's space.[^2]

| Everyday phrase | What the study is pointing at |
| --- | --- |
| "My hand feels warm" | Thermoregulatory / somatosensory processing |
| "That person seems warm" | Social-affective judgment |
| "Same neighborhood in the brain" | Overlapping anterior-insula activation in the cited design |

**Keep the fence:** neural overlap is the more durable claim in the sources' framing. Downstream gift-choice behavior is the fragile one (see Lynott).[^4] Embodied cognition here means *tint*, not *remote control*.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: reading Kang beside Lynott"}
Kang et al. (2011) report temperature effects on fairness/trust-related allocations—including the cited ~**+24.8%** first-mover story at ~**60°C** vs cold.[^3]

Lynott et al. (2014) fail to replicate Williams & Bargh's *gift-choice* Study 2 at high power.[^4]

Both can be true in a careful teaching site:

- Some thermal designs show social/fairness shifts.
- The most famous prosocial-gift headline did not survive a hard replication check.
- Therefore: cite warmth as **interesting and contested**, and as a **methods confound**—not as a permanent generosity switch.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: Williams & Bargh vs Kang vs Lynott (side-by-side)"}
Three papers do different jobs. Keeping them in one table stops a common slide: citing the largest original *d* while ignoring the failed replication, or treating Kang's bargaining design as if it *were* Williams & Bargh's gift choice.

| Paper | What was manipulated | What was measured | Headline number (as taught here) | Status for this site |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Williams & Bargh (2008) Study 1 | Brief warm vs cold cup | Personality "warmth" rating (1–7) | M ≈ **5.63** vs **4.04**; *d* ≈ **1.69** | Original claim—very large [^1] |
| Williams & Bargh (2008) Study 2 | Warm vs cold therapeutic pad | Gift for friend vs self | Warm **54%** friend; cold **75%** self | Original claim [^1] |
| Lynott et al. (2014) | Preregistered multi-lab repeat of Study 2 | Same gift-choice logic | **No support** at any site; combined **N = 861** | **Failed replication**—keep prominent [^4] |
| Kang et al. (2011) | Physical temperature around fairness/trust tasks | Fairness / first-mover style allocations | Cited narrative ~**+24.8%** first send at ~**60°C** vs cold | Separate design—not a Lynott rematch [^3] |
| Inagaki & Eisenberger (2013) | Warm pad + supportive messages | fMRI overlap in anterior insula | Shared insula cluster | Neural-overlap bridge [^2] |

**Teaching sentence:** the famous prosocial-gift headline is **contested**; the insula overlap is **more durable** in the sources' framing; Kang is a **different** thermal-bargaining story that Chapter 4 still treats as a reason to lock mug temperature—not as a boardroom cheat code.[^3][^4][^7]
:::

## Why Chapter 4 will obsess over 60°C

If you only remember one applied sentence from this lesson, remember this: **mug temperature is not a neutral stage prop.**

When Chapter 5's protocols lock drinks near **60°C ± 2°C** in opaque mugs, they are not being fussy for fun. They are trying to keep this lesson's thermal story from silently riding along with caffeine and [L-theanine](../../glossary.qmd#l-theanine) ([Chapter 5 · Section 4 Study protocols](../module-05/04-study-protocols.qmd)).

Context is part of the dose. Warmth is part of context.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: why the matched mug sits near 60°C"}
Chapter 4's study-protocol lesson specifies drinks in identical opaque mugs held near **60°C ± 2°C**, with bitterness matched (for example with food-grade quinine in controls) so that *temperature and taste* do not quietly become the experiment.[^7]

Why that number shows up in the sources' warmth narrative:

- Kang et al.'s temperature manipulations are taught here with a warm condition near **~60°C** versus a cold pad—so locking the mug near that band is a methods rhyme, not a mystical tea temperature.[^3]
- If thermal priming can shift *some* social or fairness behaviors in *some* designs, then an unlocked mug temperature confounds pharmacology with warmth.[^3]
- Opacity and matched bitterness attack a different confound: people guessing which cup is "the real tea."

**Not claimed:** that 60°C is the one true serving temperature for every tea style, or that locking temperature *creates* trust. It *controls* a variable this lesson made visible.
:::



## Field vs lab: what a beginner should expect

In a quiet lab, a researcher can hand you a warm pad, ask you to rate a stranger, and write down a number. In a noisy cafe, warmth competes with sleep debt, reputation, attractiveness, and whether you already like the person across from you. That is one reason large behavioral replications struggled: the original effect was huge, and huge social effects are exactly what later teams stress-test.[^4][^5]

So use this lesson as a **lens**, not a lever. The lens says: body temperature can tint social judgment, especially in stripped-down tasks. The lever fantasy says: hand someone a mug and rewrite the deal. Chapter 4 will keep the lens and refuse the fantasy.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: field vs lab — what a beginner should expect"}
| Setting | What is controlled | What usually wins | How to read a "warm mug" claim |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quiet lab | Cup temperature, task, stranger description | The experimental contrast can show up as a rating shift | Interesting *if* replicated |
| Multi-lab replication | Same idea, more sites, preregistration | Fragile effects often shrink or vanish | Lynott N = 861 is the caution light [^4] |
| Cafe / boardroom | Almost nothing thermal is locked | Sleep, liking, power, reputation, room climate | Do not sell a mug as strategy |

Source note: downstream behavioral outcomes in unstructured settings are highly moderated by individual differences (for example attachment style) and by ambient room temperature—even when the neural overlap story looks sturdier.[^2][^4]

Chabris and colleagues' later reports likewise lean near-zero for the original warmth-to-prosocial headline in field-leaning checks.[^5] That is why this site keeps Lynott in the open caution box, not buried in a footnote.
:::



::: {.callout-tip title="You can stop here"}
- A cozy mug can tint how "warm" someone seems—interesting, not magic.
- Some early lab headlines were huge; a large replication (**N = 861**) failed to copy the famous gift-choice result.
- Chapter 5 locks mug temperature near **60°C** so warmth does not quietly ride along with the drink.
- Passive warmth (hold a mug) ≠ active ritual (make the tea)—next lesson.
:::
